blocks.text: You are a Mars mission-planning analyst. Use only the supplied survey. Make one clear recommendation and do not invent measurements.

## Mission objective
The rover must reach exposed hydrated-sulfate deposits within 2.0 km of landing. The prime mission is to collect samples that can preserve evidence of ancient groundwater.

## Operating limits
The rover can safely cross slopes up to 12 degrees. The landing site must provide at least 7.0 hours of winter sunlight and at least 90% direct-to-orbiter visibility during the first 30 sols.

## Zephyr Basin
Hydrated-sulfate outcrops begin 1.8 km from the ellipse. The traverse is mostly 4–8 degrees. Winter sunlight averages 8.4 hours and orbiter visibility is 94%. A shallow dust field covers the final 300 m; wheel slip is the main remaining risk.

## Aurora Ridge
The sulfate outcrops are only 0.5 km away, but the direct route crosses repeated 15–18 degree slopes. Winter sunlight averages 6.1 hours and orbiter visibility is 88%.

## Cinder Plain
Winter sunlight averages 10.6 hours and orbiter visibility is 97%. The terrain is nearly flat, but orbital spectroscopy found no hydrated-sulfate exposure within 6 km.

## Available mitigation
Mission control can reserve two sols for a low-speed wheel-slip survey and route the rover around the southern edge of Zephyr's dust field, adding 0.4 km to the traverse.

## Request
Write a 140–180 word landing recommendation. Open with the selected site. Explain how it meets the science, mobility, power, and communications requirements; identify the main remaining risk and its mitigation; then close by comparing the two rejected sites. Use one compact paragraph with no heading.

answer.text: The recommended landing site is Zephyr Basin, as it satisfies all mission constraints while offering the best balance of science and safety. It meets the science requirement with hydrated-sulfate outcrops located 1.8 km away, well within the 2.0 km limit, and preserves evidence of ancient groundwater. Mobility is assured since the traverse slopes range from 4 to 8 degrees, staying safely under the 12-degree limit. Power and communications needs are fully met with 8.4 hours of winter sunlight and 94% orbiter visibility, exceeding the minimum thresholds of 7.0 hours and 90%. The primary remaining risk is wheel slip within the final 300 meters of a shallow dust field, which can be effectively mitigated by reserving two sols for a low-speed survey and routing around the southern edge of the dust field, adding only 0.4 km to the traverse. This site is superior to Aurora Ridge, where steep 15–18 degree slopes exceed mobility limits and insufficient sunlight and visibility fail operational requirements. Furthermore, Cinder Plain is rejected because orbital spectroscopy confirms no hydrated-sulfate exposure within 6 km, rendering it scientifically unviable for the prime objective.
